title: A single GitHub Issue could hijack Claude Code and Gemini CLI runs — Black Hat research lands two CVEs, one at CVSS 10.0
subtitle: Novee researcher Elad Meged's August 5 Black Hat talk detailed harness-layer flaws in three flagship coding agents; Anthropic patched, Google shipped a breaking trust-model change, and OpenAI declined to issue a CVE for Codex.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: At Black Hat USA 2026 in Las Vegas on August 5, Novee founding engineer Elad Meged disclosed a set of vulnerabilities that let an unprivileged attacker take control of runs by Anthropic's Claude Code, Google's Gemini CLI, and OpenAI's Codex simply by placing malicious content in a public GitHub Issue, a repository file, or a container-launch environment file. The Claude Code flaw, assigned CVE-2026-54316, turned Hugging Face's public download counter into a covert exfiltration channel that leaked an API key one character at a time. Every Claude Code release from 0.2.54 through 2.1.162 is affected; the fix ships in 2.1.163. The Gemini CLI vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-12537, is an OS command injection reached through a crafted `.gemini/.env` file inside the container launcher — Google rated it CVSS v4 10.0 and shipped a breaking change to its trust model for non-interactive execution environments. The Codex finding produced no version-specific patch and no CVE; OpenAI's position, per Novee, is that its sandbox behaved as documented.

The recurring pattern across all three products was not a model failure. It was a harness failure — the code around the model that decides what actually gets executed on the host. In each case one component of the harness marked an attacker-influenced value as safe, and a later component in the same pipeline consumed that value with greater authority than the first component had assumed. In the Gemini CLI case, that meant a `.env` file read by the container launcher could inject shell commands that ran outside the sandbox. In the Claude Code case, an agent that was allowed to make outbound HTTP requests to Hugging Face was allowed to encode secrets in the request pattern itself. None of these require jailbreaking the model. They require getting the model to touch attacker-controlled data at the right point in a workflow that already has legitimate elevated permissions.

The disclosure timing matters. All three vendors were notified in advance under coordinated disclosure, but the industry response bifurcated: Anthropic patched multiple times through the disclosure window and assigned a CVE, Google took the maximum-severity rating and shipped a breaking change (which will force existing Gemini CLI users to update their configuration), and OpenAI treated the finding as expected sandbox behaviour and did not ship a version bump. That split will shape how enterprises evaluate agent products for the next quarter. It also reinforces a point that the Open Secure AI Alliance's SAFE framework from August 4 was designed for: coding agents ingest text from many sources — issues, comments, wikis, container env files, CI logs — and each of those sources is a plausible ingress path for prompt-injection-style attacks that end in real code execution on real machines. Novee's takeaway line to the Black Hat audience was that most teams running these agents in production have not yet reduced the write-token scope in their GitHub Actions runners.

For learners: if you deploy any coding agent — Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, whatever comes next — read its security model before you wire it to your CI. The model itself is the safest part of the system. The harness around it, the tools it can call, the tokens it inherits from the runner, and the data sources you let it touch are the parts that get exploited. Two low-cost, high-return moves you can make today: strip write permissions from any PR-triggered workflow that runs an agent, and pin agent versions rather than tracking `latest` — so the next fix, or the next regression, is a change you notice.
